title: HCF and LCM
subtitle: Quantitative Aptitude – Placement Preparation
description: Learn factors, multiples, prime factorization, HCF, LCM, division methods, relationships between numbers and common placement aptitude applications.
learningObjectives: Find the HCF of two or more numbers.
Find the LCM of two or more numbers.
Use prime factorization to calculate HCF and LCM.
Use the division method to calculate HCF.
Use the common-division method to calculate LCM.
Apply the relationship between HCF, LCM and the product of two numbers.
Find unknown numbers using HCF and LCM.
Solve recurring-event and timing problems using LCM.
Find the HCF and LCM of fractions.
Apply shortcuts commonly used in placement aptitude tests.

sections.heading: 1. Factors and Multiples
content: A factor of a number divides that number exactly without leaving a remainder.
A multiple of a number is obtained by multiplying the number by a whole number.
Every positive integer has at least two factors: 1 and the number itself.
A number has a finite number of factors but infinitely many multiples.
formulas: If a divides b exactly, then a is a factor of b
Multiples of n = n, 2n, 3n, 4n, ...

examples.question: List all the factors of 18.
examples.solution: The factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18.

examples.question: Write the first five positive multiples of 7.
examples.solution: The first five positive multiples are 7, 14, 21, 28 and 35.

sections.heading: 2. Prime and Composite Numbers
content: A prime number has exactly two positive factors: 1 and itself.
A composite number has more than two positive factors.
The number 1 is neither prime nor composite.
Prime factorization expresses a number as a product of prime numbers.
formulas: Prime number: exactly two positive factors
Composite number: more than two positive factors

examples.question: Determine whether 29 is prime or composite.
examples.solution: The only factors of 29 are 1 and 29. Therefore, 29 is prime.

examples.question: Write the prime factorization of 60.

sections.heading: 3. Meaning of HCF
content: HCF stands for Highest Common Factor.
It is also called the Greatest Common Divisor or GCD.
The HCF is the greatest positive integer that divides each of the given numbers exactly.
HCF is commonly used in grouping, cutting and maximum-size problems.
formulas: HCF = Greatest factor common to all the given numbers
HCF is always less than or equal to the smallest given number

examples.question: Find the HCF of 12 and 18 by listing factors.
examples.solution: Factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. Factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18. The greatest common factor is 6.

examples.question: Find the HCF of 20 and 30.
examples.solution: The common factors are 1, 2, 5 and 10. Therefore, the HCF is 10.

sections.heading: 4. Meaning of LCM
content: LCM stands for Least Common Multiple.
It is the smallest positive number that is exactly divisible by all the given numbers.
LCM is useful in recurring-event, scheduling, repetition and synchronization problems.
The LCM is always greater than or equal to the largest given number.
formulas: LCM = Smallest positive multiple common to all the given numbers

examples.question: Find the LCM of 4 and 6 by listing multiples.
examples.solution: Multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16 and so on. Multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18 and so on. The first common multiple is 12.

examples.question: Find the LCM of 5 and 8.
examples.solution: The smallest number divisible by both 5 and 8 is 40. Therefore, the LCM is 40.

sections.heading: 5. HCF Using Prime Factorization
content: Express each number as a product of prime factors.
Select only the prime factors common to all the numbers.
For every common prime factor, take the smallest exponent.
Multiply the selected factors to obtain the HCF.
formulas: HCF = Product of common prime factors with the smallest powers

examples.question: Find the HCF of 36 and 48 using prime factorization.
examples.solution: 36 = 2^2 × 3^2 and 48 = 2^4 × 3. Common factors with minimum powers are 2^2 × 3 = 12.

examples.question: Find the HCF of 24, 36 and 60.

sections.heading: 6. LCM Using Prime Factorization
content: Express every number as a product of prime factors.
Include every prime factor that appears in any of the numbers.
For every prime factor, take the greatest exponent.
Multiply the selected factors to obtain the LCM.
formulas: LCM = Product of all prime factors with the greatest powers

examples.question: Find the LCM of 36 and 48 using prime factorization.
Find the LCM of 12, 18 and 30.

sections.heading: 7. HCF Using the Division Method
content: Divide the larger number by the smaller number.
Replace the larger number with the smaller number and the smaller number with the remainder.
Continue until the remainder becomes zero.
The last non-zero divisor is the HCF.
formulas: Dividend = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder
HCF(a, b) = HCF(b, remainder)

examples.question: Find the HCF of 252 and 105 using the division method.
Find the HCF of 867 and 255.

sections.heading: 8. LCM Using the Common-Division Method
content: Write the numbers together and divide them by suitable prime numbers.
A prime may divide one, some or all the numbers.
Continue until every remaining value becomes 1.
Multiply all the divisors to obtain the LCM.
formulas: LCM = Product of all prime divisors used in the common-division process

examples.question: Find the LCM of 12, 15 and 20.
examples.solution: Using successive prime divisors 2, 2, 3 and 5, the LCM is 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 60.

examples.question: Find the LCM of 8, 18 and 24.
examples.solution: The highest prime powers required are 2^3 and 3^2. Therefore, LCM = 8 × 9 = 72.

sections.heading: 9. Relationship Between HCF and LCM
content: For any two positive integers, the product of the numbers equals the product of their HCF and LCM.
This relationship applies directly to two numbers.
It should not be applied in the same simple form to three or more numbers.
formulas: First number × Second number = HCF × LCM
LCM = Product of two numbers / HCF
HCF = Product of two numbers / LCM

examples.question: The HCF of two numbers is 6 and their LCM is 180. If one number is 30, find the other.
examples.solution: Other number = (6 × 180)/30 = 36.

examples.question: Find the LCM of 24 and 36 if their HCF is 12.

sections.heading: 10. Co-Prime Numbers
content: Two numbers are co-prime when their HCF is 1.
Co-prime numbers do not need to be prime individually.
Consecutive positive integers are always co-prime.
For two co-prime numbers, the LCM equals their product.
formulas: For co-prime numbers, HCF = 1
For co-prime numbers, LCM = Product of the numbers

examples.question: Are 8 and 15 co-prime?
examples.solution: The only common factor of 8 and 15 is 1. Therefore, they are co-prime.

examples.question: Find the LCM of 9 and 20.
examples.solution: Since 9 and 20 are co-prime, LCM = 9 × 20 = 180.

sections.heading: 11. Finding Numbers from HCF and LCM
content: If the HCF of two numbers is H, represent the numbers as Hx and Hy.
The values x and y must be co-prime.
The LCM of the numbers becomes Hxy.
This representation helps identify possible number pairs.
formulas: Numbers = Hx and Hy, where HCF(x, y) = 1
LCM = Hxy
xy = LCM/HCF

examples.question: The HCF of two numbers is 6 and their LCM is 210. Find a possible pair of numbers.
examples.solution: xy = 210/6 = 35. Co-prime factor pairs of 35 include 5 and 7. Therefore, the numbers can be 6 × 5 = 30 and 6 × 7 = 42.

examples.question: The HCF is 8 and the LCM is 96. If the numbers are in the ratio 2:3, find them.
examples.solution: Let the numbers be 8 × 2 and 8 × 3 because 2 and 3 are co-prime. Therefore, the numbers are 16 and 24.

sections.heading: 12. Greatest Number That Divides Given Numbers Exactly
content: When a question asks for the greatest number that divides several numbers exactly, calculate their HCF.
The word greatest generally indicates HCF in exact-division problems.
formulas: Greatest exact divisor = HCF of the given numbers

examples.question: Find the greatest number that divides 84, 126 and 210 exactly.
examples.solution: HCF of 84, 126 and 210 is 42. Therefore, the required number is 42.

examples.question: Find the greatest number that divides 96, 144 and 240 without leaving a remainder.
examples.solution: HCF of 96, 144 and 240 is 48.

sections.heading: 13. Greatest Number Leaving the Same Remainder
content: If a divisor leaves the same remainder when dividing several numbers, subtract the numbers pairwise.
The required greatest divisor is the HCF of those differences.
The common remainder must be smaller than the required divisor.
formulas: Required divisor = HCF of pairwise differences

examples.question: Find the greatest number that divides 43, 91 and 183 leaving the same remainder.
examples.solution: Differences are 91 − 43 = 48, 183 − 91 = 92 and 183 − 43 = 140. HCF of 48, 92 and 140 is 4.

examples.question: Find the greatest number that divides 65, 81 and 97 leaving the same remainder.
examples.solution: Differences are 16, 16 and 32. Their HCF is 16. Therefore, the required divisor is 16.

sections.heading: 14. Greatest Number Leaving Specified Remainders
content: When different numbers leave specified remainders, subtract each remainder from its corresponding number.
The required greatest divisor is the HCF of the resulting values.
Confirm that each given remainder is smaller than the divisor.
formulas: Required divisor = HCF(Number1 − Remainder1, Number2 − Remainder2, ...)

examples.question: Find the greatest number that divides 187 and 233 leaving remainders 7 and 8 respectively.
Find the greatest number that divides 122, 186 and 250 leaving remainder 2 in each case.
examples.solution: Subtract 2 from each number: 120, 184 and 248. Their HCF is 8.

sections.heading: 15. Least Number Divisible by Given Numbers
content: When a question asks for the smallest or least number divisible by several given numbers, calculate their LCM.
The words least, smallest, together again and next common occurrence usually indicate LCM.
formulas: Least exactly divisible number = LCM of the given numbers

examples.question: Find the least number exactly divisible by 12, 15 and 18.
examples.solution: LCM of 12, 15 and 18 is 180.

examples.question: Find the smallest number divisible by 8, 10 and 12.

sections.heading: 16. Least Number Leaving a Common Remainder
content: First calculate the LCM of the given divisors.
Add the common remainder to the LCM.
This works when the same remainder is required for every divisor.
formulas: Required least number = LCM of divisors + Common remainder

examples.question: Find the least number that leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4, 6 and 8.
examples.solution: LCM of 4, 6 and 8 is 24. Required number = 24 + 3 = 27.

examples.question: Find the least number that leaves remainder 5 when divided by 6, 8 and 12.
examples.solution: LCM of 6, 8 and 12 is 24. Required number = 24 + 5 = 29.

sections.heading: 17. Least Number Requiring an Addition or Subtraction
content: Find the LCM of the given divisors first.
If a number must leave a common remainder, add that remainder.
If a number is less than a required multiple by a fixed value, subtract that value from the LCM.
Check the final number against all the conditions.
formulas: Number leaving remainder r = Multiple of LCM + r
Number requiring addition k = Multiple of LCM − k

examples.question: Find the least number that must be increased by 5 to become divisible by 12, 18 and 24.
examples.solution: LCM of 12, 18 and 24 is 72. Required number = 72 − 5 = 67.

examples.question: Find the least number that must be decreased by 4 to become divisible by 6, 8 and 10.
examples.solution: LCM of 6, 8 and 10 is 120. Required number = 120 + 4 = 124.

sections.heading: 18. Recurring Events and Time Intervals
content: When events repeat after fixed intervals, use LCM to determine when they occur together again.
Convert all intervals into the same unit before calculating the LCM.
If the events occur together at the starting time, add the LCM interval to that time.
formulas: Time until events occur together again = LCM of their intervals

examples.question: Three bells ring every 6, 8 and 12 minutes. If they ring together now, after how many minutes will they ring together again?
examples.solution: LCM of 6, 8 and 12 is 24. They will ring together again after 24 minutes.

examples.question: Three traffic lights change every 30, 45 and 60 seconds. After how many seconds will they change together again?
examples.solution: LCM of 30, 45 and 60 is 180 seconds.

sections.heading: 19. HCF and LCM of Fractions
content: For fractions, first ensure that every fraction is in its lowest form.
The HCF of fractions uses the HCF of numerators and the LCM of denominators.
The LCM of fractions uses the LCM of numerators and the HCF of denominators.
formulas: HCF of fractions = HCF of numerators / LCM of denominators
LCM of fractions = LCM of numerators / HCF of denominators

examples.question: Find the HCF of 2/3 and 4/9.
examples.solution: HCF of numerators 2 and 4 is 2. LCM of denominators 3 and 9 is 9. Therefore, HCF = 2/9.

examples.question: Find the LCM of 3/4 and 5/6.
examples.solution: LCM of numerators 3 and 5 is 15. HCF of denominators 4 and 6 is 2. Therefore, LCM = 15/2.

sections.heading: 20. Placement-Test Strategy
content: Use HCF for greatest-size, maximum-grouping, cutting and exact-division questions.
Use LCM for least-number, repeated-event and synchronization questions.
For same-remainder questions, calculate the HCF of the differences.
For a common remainder with several divisors, calculate the LCM and add the remainder.
Use the product relationship only when exactly two numbers are involved.
Check whether the numbers are co-prime before multiplying them directly for the LCM.
Use prime factorization when several numbers are given.
Use the Euclidean division method for large numbers.
Read words such as greatest, least, together again and maximum carefully.
formulas: For two numbers: Product = HCF × LCM
Same remainder: HCF of differences
Recurring events: LCM of intervals
Numbers with HCF H: Hx and Hy, where x and y are co-prime

examples.question: Two numbers have HCF 12 and LCM 420. If one number is 60, find the other.
examples.solution: Other number = (12 × 420)/60 = 84.

examples.question: Three machines operate every 12, 18 and 30 minutes. If they start together, when will they operate together again?
examples.solution: LCM of 12, 18 and 30 is 180 minutes, which is 3 hours.

quickShortcuts.title: Greatest exact divisor
quickShortcuts.note: Use the HCF of the given numbers.

quickShortcuts.title: Least divisible number
quickShortcuts.note: Use the LCM of the given numbers.

quickShortcuts.title: Prime-factor HCF
quickShortcuts.note: Take only common prime factors with their smallest powers.

quickShortcuts.title: Prime-factor LCM
quickShortcuts.note: Take all required prime factors with their greatest powers.

quickShortcuts.title: Two-number relationship
quickShortcuts.note: Product of two numbers equals HCF multiplied by LCM.

quickShortcuts.title: Find the second number
quickShortcuts.note: Second number = HCF × LCM ÷ First number.

quickShortcuts.title: Co-prime numbers
quickShortcuts.note: Their HCF is 1 and their LCM is their product.

quickShortcuts.title: Consecutive numbers
quickShortcuts.note: Any two consecutive positive integers are co-prime.

quickShortcuts.title: Same remainder
quickShortcuts.note: Take the HCF of the pairwise differences.

quickShortcuts.title: Specified remainders
quickShortcuts.note: Subtract each remainder first and then calculate the HCF.

quickShortcuts.title: Common remainder
quickShortcuts.note: Required least number is usually LCM plus the common remainder.

quickShortcuts.title: Recurring events
quickShortcuts.note: Use the LCM of the time intervals.

quickShortcuts.title: Maximum equal groups
quickShortcuts.note: Use HCF when every group must have the same composition.

quickShortcuts.title: Largest equal piece
quickShortcuts.note: Use HCF for cutting lengths into the largest equal pieces.

quickShortcuts.title: HCF of fractions
quickShortcuts.note: HCF of numerators divided by LCM of denominators.

quickShortcuts.title: LCM of fractions
quickShortcuts.note: LCM of numerators divided by HCF of denominators.

Assuming that all odd numbers are prime.
Assuming that co-prime numbers must both be prime.
Forgetting that 1 is neither prime nor composite.
Using LCM for a greatest-size grouping problem.
Using HCF for a recurring-event problem.
Failing to subtract the remainders before finding HCF.
Adding a remainder when the question requires subtraction.
Not converting all time intervals into the same unit.
Multiplying numbers directly without checking whether they are co-prime.
Using unreduced fractions in HCF and LCM fraction questions.
Forgetting to verify the final number against all given conditions.
